You are a language model whose weights can be adapted with LoRA adapters. On this site the policy that is trained and scored is Tinker's hosted copy of the base model with your LoRA adapters. Your workspace is …/efeS2_golf_s41/workspace.
Each reply is run as one bash command; if it contains a ```bash block, the last one is run.
You see the command result (up to 20000 characters; longer output shows its head and tail) and environment observations.
A command still running after 600 s is killed with everything it started, and you see "timed out after 600s" with its output so far.
Read ENVIRONMENT.json for the tasks, budget and enforced constraints and STATUS.json for the current state; read
skills/tools/SKILL.md and skills/trainer/SKILL.md for tool usage and the installed trainer's spec.
The objective is the total hidden-seed success count across all tasks of the scored policy.
The hidden seeds are disjoint from every seed you can train or evaluate on; a success rate measured on seeds a policy was
trained on overstates its rate on held-out seeds.
`python3 finish.py` ends the session in two steps: it submits a policy (by default the loaded one; `load.py unload` with no
names loads the base) and prints exactly what will be scored, and `python3 finish.py --confirm TOKEN` in a later turn ends
the session. Budget exhaustion and operator caps also end the session; the environment then scores your pending
submission, else the loaded policy.
Mission (facts of this environment):
- You and the policy: the policy is a separate model; loading adapters changes only it, never you.
- Objective: the hidden-seed successes of the policy you submit, within the GPU-hour budget (ENVIRONMENT.json `evaluation`).
- A practice call (train.py): the task's official eval prompt goes to the policy, the policy writes programs, each program runs in the simulator and gets a practice reward, and the rewards train a LoRA adapter.
- Adapters: every train adds an adapter to your library; load.py loads one adapter or a stack (a single adapter per eval on this site (Tinker samples one trained state)), a merge you can dev-evaluate with eval.py before you submit; `load.py unload` removes them.
- Final evaluation: the one stack you submit (finish.py) serves every task.
- Boundaries: the policy gets no privileged information at evaluation (only each task's eval prompt and scene); every train and eval call is charged to the budget.

# embodied-olympics golf-putt — instance i00

You control a simulated Unitree G1 humanoid robot (29 joints, 1.32 m tall, 34 kg; the Embodied Olympics simulator on MuJoCo)
via Python. **Task:** Hole the 3.0 m putt: with one stroke of the putter in your right hand, roll the golf ball that lies on the green into the hole.

This is a *fixed instance*: the same venue and start every time. You may reset and retry as many times as you want.
Your deliverable is **one replayable trajectory**, not a general policy.

## The venue
You stand on the green facing +x, side-on to the putt as a golfer does. The ball lies 0.44 m ahead of your pelvis and -0.12 m to your left (negative: to your right); the hole's centre is 3.0 m from the ball in the +y direction (to your left), so the line of play runs across in front of your feet. The green is level and extends 1.5 m behind the ball (to your right), 3.0 m beyond the hole and 2.0 m to each side of the line of play; around it the ground is 0.1016 m lower. The putter is a blade putter: its grip is held in your right fist at right angles to the forearm, the butt 0.05 m above the fist and the shaft leaving the fist on the other side, so with your arm at rest it points away from your right side, about level with your hand. The head (0.110 m from heel to toe, 0.025 m from face to back, 0.025 m high, 0.35 kg) sits at the shaft's end at a lie of 70 degrees, its toe on the side your forearm points to; its face looks at right angles to both the shaft and the forearm: to your left when the forearm points forwards and the shaft down. There is no wind.

Frame: metres; the origin is on the floor under your pelvis at the start, +x is the way you face at the start, +y is
to your left, +z is up; the floor is z = 0. 

## The rules
**Rule book:** The Rules of Golf (R&A / USGA, 2023): Definitions "Hole", "Holed", "Stroke", "Line of Play"; Rules 8.1b, 9.4, 10.1a, 10.1c, 11.1, 13.2, 13.3a; the Equipment Rules (2023), Part 2 (clubs) and Part 4 (the ball); the USGA Stimpmeter instructions for the green's speed. Where this task departs from it:

- Definition "Hole": the opening is a regular 24-sided polygon inscribed in the 0.108 m circle (flats 0.5 mm inside it, never wider than the official hole) with rigid vertical walls (the liner is only drawn), because the simulator has no cylindrical cavity
- Rule 13.2: there is no flagstick (as when the player has it removed)
- Rule 10.1 and the Equipment Rules on the grip: the putter is fixed rigidly to the right wrist of a robot that has no fingers, its grip at right angles to the forearm (as a fist holds a hammer), and is played with one arm; the club itself is not scaled to the 1.32 m robot
- Rule 10.1a (a fair strike; an accidental double hit is one stroke): the referee needs numbers: every contact of the head with the ball must fall within 0.2 s of the first, and the contacts together may last at most 0.03 s (the simulated impact of a clean putt lasts 0.012 s, a real one 0.0005 s: the ball's contact is softer than a real ball's so that the simulator's 1 ms step resolves it)
- Rules 9.4, 11.1 and 3.3 (penalty strokes, replaying, counting strokes): a single attempt: anything that would cost a penalty or need a second stroke ends it as a failure
- Rule 13.3a (waiting for a ball that overhangs the hole): a ball that has been at rest for 1.0 s is final
- the green: perfectly flat and uniform, no grain, no wind; its speed (stimp 10) is the ball's rolling resistance, calibrated so that a ball rolling at 1.83 m/s stops after 3.05 m

The ball (42.67 mm, 45.9 g) lies at rest on a flat green of stimp 10 (a ball that starts rolling at 1.83 m/s stops after 3.05 m). The hole is cut into the green 3.0 m from the ball: 0.108 m across and 0.1016 m deep, with no flagstick in it. A putter (0.86 m long, 0.5 kg, 3.0 degrees of loft) is fixed in your right hand. You succeed when the ball is holed with one stroke: after the stroke it comes to rest (its centre moves less than 0.001 m in 1.0 s) inside the hole with the whole ball below the surface of the green. A stroke is a fair strike of the ball with the putter's head (any side of the head): the first contact of the head with the ball starts it, every further contact must come within 0.2 s of the first (an accidental double hit is still one stroke), and all the contacts together may last at most 0.03 s. You fail if the contacts last longer (the ball was pushed, scraped or scooped), if the head touches the ball again later (a second stroke), if anything else of you ever touches the ball (the putter's shaft or grip, a foot, a leg, a hand), if at the moment of the stroke your feet touch the green on both sides of the line of play (the straight line through the ball's spot and the hole's centre, extended behind the ball) or on that line, if the ball comes to rest anywhere but in the hole (on the lip and on the green beyond the hole included), if the ball leaves the green, if you fall (your pelvis lower than 0.35 m above the green, or any part of you other than your feet touching the ground; the putter may touch the green), or after 30 s.

A referee decides this from the simulator's state after every physics step (1 ms): the events that must happen, in
order, are **stroke → holed**. The attempt ends at the success (that moment is the success), at the first rule violation,
or after 30 s (3000 control steps). `s.status()` shows the referee's record at any time:
`stages`, `failed` (the rule that ended the attempt), `metrics`, `events`.

## Deliverable
Leave two files under `/app/output/`. **Only the first is scored**; the other is how a human reads your work
afterwards, so keep it short and factual.

| file | what goes in it |
|---|---|
| `trajectory.npz` | the trajectory, written with `s.save_trajectory()` (below): `actions`, one sim row of 151 floats per control step. Replayed open-loop from the frozen start in two fresh processes, one row per control step until the referee ends the attempt; scored 1 if both replays succeed and end in the same state, else 0. The rows must reach the success: when they run out the attempt is judged as it stands. At most 3000 rows are used; every one of them must be finite, also those after the attempt's end (a file with a NaN or an infinite value scores 0) |
| `gen.py` | the script that produced it. It must **run and reproduce `trajectory.npz`**, reading nothing but `/app/instance.json` and files under `/app/output/` |

The tooling also appends its own log, `rcb_session_log.jsonl`, to `/app/output/`: leave it there and do not set
`RCB_SESSION_LOG`.

**Write `trajectory.npz` as soon as you have any trajectory at all, and overwrite it (with `gen.py` to
match) whenever you have a better one.** A run
that ends with no file scores zero.

Goal: Hole the 3.0 m putt: with one stroke of the putter in your right hand, roll the golf ball that lies on the green into the hole.
Write ONLY executable Python code: no prose, no shell commands, no code fences; comments allowed. It is one program that runs once, as /app/output/gen.py in the task's container described above, for at most 300 s; only the /app/output/trajectory.npz it writes is scored.

name: trainer
description: The EFE trainer contract: every field train.py reads, what each failure returns, costs, and what a train produces.
---
# Trainer on this site (Embodied First Exam tasks; Tinker practice, task containers local)

`python3 train.py SPEC` submits one practice call; SPEC is a JSON or YAML file in the workspace.
Relative adapter names in SPEC resolve against the workspace's adapters.

## What a practice call is
GRPO on a LoRA adapter (rank 32, alpha 64) of Qwen3.8-27B as hosted on Tinker, sampled and updated there; every program runs on
this cluster. Each step: `batch` prompts x `rollouts` rollouts, one optimizer update (AdamW). Prompt k of the call is the next task
of `task` (in the order given) on seed `seed_start + k x rollouts`; all rollouts of one prompt run on that same instance. A rollout
is one program written for the task: it runs once in the task's container for at most 300 s, then the task's own verifier replays
the trajectory it wrote and checks the end state. The training prompt is the task's evaluation prompt. Sampling: temperature 1.0,
top_p 0.95, top_k 20, thinking off, at most 8192 tokens.

## Rewards
| `reward` | value of one rollout | tasks |
|---|---|---|
| `success` | 1.0 if the verifier's success check passes, else 0.0 | every task |
| `progress` | the referee's stages reached / stages total (0.0 to 1.0) | Embodied Olympics tasks only |
| `shaped` | Meta-World's own shaped reward of the state after the last action (the verifier's `final_reward`, 0 to 10) divided by 10 (0.0 to 1.0) | MetaWorld+ tasks only |

A program that crashes, runs past its time limit or writes no trajectory gets 0.0. The reward is for practice calls only: `eval.py` and the hidden evaluation count successes, whatever reward a train used.

## Spec fields (any other field is refused)
| field | type | default | accepted |
|---|---|---|---|
| `task` | string or list | required | task names from tasks.json |
| `steps` | integer | 1 | any positive integer |
| `batch` | integer | 8 | prompts per step |
| `rollouts` | integer | 8 | rollouts per prompt: 4, 8 or 16 |
| `seed_start` | integer | 810001 | prompt k runs on seed `seed_start + k x rollouts`; the call's seeds must not reach seeds 1-100 |
| `lr` | number | 2e-05 | in (0, 1e-3] |
| `reward` | string | `success` | `success`, `progress` or `shaped` (table above) |
| `init` | string | omitted: a fresh LoRA | an adapter name produced by an earlier train of this session; the call continues from its weights |

## Failures
A request this site cannot run as written ends `failed` with this text; nothing is charged:
- `train: unknown spec field(s) [<fields>]; this site reads [<fields>]`
- `train: task must be a task name from tasks.json or a list of them`
- `train: task '<name>' is not an EFE task of this site`
- `train: <field> must be a positive integer, got <value>`
- `train: rollouts must be one of [4, 8, 16], got <value>`
- `train: lr must be in (0, 1e-3], got <value>`
- `train: reward '<mode>': <task> (<suite>) has no '<mode>' reward; use one of [<modes>]`
- `train: <task> is a held-out task (protocol efe-dev (not the EFE leaderboard setting)): it is scored only at the final evaluation`
- `train: seeds 1-100 are reserved for the final score; use dev seeds >= 800001`
- `train: init '<name>': trainer=tinker continues only adapters it trained (their training.json names a tinker_state); train from the base instead`
- `refused: Tinker budget exhausted (ledger <x> / cap <y> USD)` (the job is `refused`, as for a GPU-hour refusal)
A failure inside the trainer or a task container ends the session as an infrastructure fault.

## Evaluation on this site
One adapter per eval is this site's design for EFE DEV (Tinker samples one trained state).
`eval.py` scores one adapter at a time (or the base model with none loaded): a stack of two or more adapters ends `failed` with
`eval: this site evaluates one adapter at a time (Tinker samples one trained state); load one adapter`. Evaluation decoding:
temperature 0.7, top_p 0.8, top_k 20, thinking off, at most 8192 tokens.

## Progress and cancel
While a train runs, its record shows whether the job is queued or running. `cancel.py ID` stops the job; no adapter is kept.

## Cost
GPU-hours as charged: the call's one CPU job, `1 x (0.055 + 0.127 x N x batch / 8 x rollouts / 8)` for a train of N steps.

| call | canonical cost |
|---|---|
| train, 1 step | 0.18 |
| train, 10 steps | 1.32 |
| train, 30 steps | 3.87 |
| train, 10 steps, `rollouts` 16 | 2.60 |
| train, N steps | 1 x (0.055 + 0.127 x N x batch / 8 x rollouts / 8) |

| eval of one task on | 5 seeds | 20 seeds | 100 seeds |
|---|---|---|---|
| canonical cost | 0.02 | 0.04 | 0.12 |

## Output
The adapter directory holds `adapter_model.safetensors`, `adapter_config.json`, `rewards.json` (per-step mean reward and fraction
of rollouts with reward > 0), `call.json` (job, GPU-hours, the Tinker state, timing, the seeds used) and `training.json`.

---
name: retrain-tools
description: Submit training and evaluation jobs, inspect results, and select the policy to score.
---

# Environment tools

Read `ENVIRONMENT.json` for the site's policy, adapter composition and enforced constraints, and `tasks.json`
for task details. `STATUS.json` contains the latest budget, loaded stack, adapters and running job IDs.
`SCOREBOARD.md` has dev scores and lineage. While a train or eval is submitted, `jobs/<id>.json` (`progress`, `progress_line`; `status.py`),
STATUS.json (`job_progress`) and the scoreboard show whether it is queued (not started, with its queue time so far) or running, and for a
running train its completed steps, latest mean reward and GPU-hours so far, as the site reports them. `tasks/<task>/eval_prompt.txt` (when
the site provides it) is the prompt the policy receives at evaluation; training prompts are checked against it. `tasks/INDEX.md` lists each task's goal line, dev and
hidden seed ranges, recorded base score, API names and key rules, taken from tasks.json, the eval prompts and the base scores. State comes from the environment; this skill is editable guidance.

| Command | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `python3 train.py SPEC` | Submit JSON/YAML spec to the installed trainer; see `skills/trainer/SKILL.md`. |
| `python3 eval.py --adapter A[,B...]\|base\|loaded --task T --seeds N` | Evaluate on the next N unused dev seeds (the result lists them; the base column has its own) with the task's `tasks/<task>/eval_prompt.txt` verbatim (no training `note`/`goal`; the final score uses the same prompt). A stack's score on a task is known only from an eval of that stack (`--adapter A,B`); neither the scoreboard nor the environment derives it from its adapters' single scores. `loaded` is the stack loaded when the request is picked up, so not an adapter whose train is still running. Results are written only when all seeds finish, so an eval that reaches its time limit usually fails with no count (rarely: a count over the seeds that finished, with `partial`). Where the site can resume an eval (eval port dq-t1v2), an eval stopped by the cluster (time limit, preemption, node failure) continues its remaining seeds in a new Slurm job, at most 3 times; its status then says `continued from seed k in job J`, and its result lists every Slurm job (`jobs`) and each continuation (`continued`: `job` stopped, `cause`, `from` seed, `of` seeds, `continued_in` job), as it lists site retries. |
| `python3 load.py load A [B...]` | Replace the loaded stack (names separated by spaces; eval.py separates them by commas). |
| `python3 load.py stack A [B...]` | Append to the loaded stack. |
| `python3 load.py unload [A...]` | Remove names, or return to base with no names. |
| `python3 status.py [ID...]` | Read job states and results; no IDs shows all jobs. The last line states what finishing now would score. |
| `python3 wait.py all\|ID... [--max 4h\|90m]` | Submit a wait barrier: your next turn starts when those jobs finish or after `--max` (default 2h), whichever comes first. If the bound comes first, the result states each job's queue state, reason, position and time pending, and "no job finished". The barrier runs in the environment after your command returns, so `--max` is not limited by the per-command time limit. |
| `python3 finish.py [--policy base \| --adapters A[,B...]] [--note TEXT]` | Step one of ending the session: submit the policy to score (no policy arguments: the loaded stack; single mode: `current`, `v<k>` or `current@<k>`). The result states exactly what will be scored and a token. |
| `python3 finish.py --confirm TOKEN` | Step two, in a later turn: end the session; the submission is scored. |
| `python3 cancel.py ID` | Stop a running train or eval. A train keeps the adapter of its last saved step (if the site saved one), registered with the steps it ran; the job is charged the GPU time it used. |

Scripts submit request files and return IDs. Shell success means submission, not job success. In the chat backend,
requests are handled only after the entire command returns: `train.py spec.json; wait.py all; load.py load a1`
queues a dependency chain, but reading status later in that same shell still sees the old state. The Codex backend has a background executor; request processing and status refresh happen independently.
